english.html: I am not moved by tears: I have been caught by that art before. You are always weeping, Cynthia, to lay a snare.

notes.original: Nil moueor lachrymis, iſta ſum capus ab arte. Semper ab inſidiis, Cynthia flere ſoles.
notes.gloss: Nil moveor lacrimis: ista sum captus ab arte; / semper ab insidiis, Cynthia, flere soles — the poet's farewell to Cynthia, the last elegy of book 3, as the orphan note a2 on p106 says.

english.html: And in truth, because women seem to be born to weep, and shed tears when it pleases them and seems good to them <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>,

notes.gloss: Jason to Medea: a woman is a female thing and born to tears (γυνὴ δὲ θῆλυ κἀπὶ δακρύοις ἔφυ).

english.html: They learn to weep becomingly, and they cry at whatever time they wish, and in whatever manner <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>.

notes.original: Ouid. au iij de arte amãd.
notes.gloss: Quo non ars penetrat? discunt lacrimare decenter, / quoque volunt plorant tempore quoque modo; the print's Quóq; is quoque with the -que sign. The `⟨alt⟩` iij⟨alt:iiij⟩ is taken as iij: the lines are in book 3, and the Ars has only three books.

english.html: One must not at all give credence to their tears, most often feigned, simulated and full of hypocrisy, nor to their words either: for women have (says Plautus) honey on their tongues; but their heart is all covered with gall, sprinkled with vinegar, full of every bitterness <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>.

notes.gloss: In melle sunt linguae sitae vostrae atque orationes, / facta atque corda in felle sunt sita atque acerbo aceto. The print's Tuſcul. is a misprint for Trucul.; the `⟨alt⟩` is taken as Plaute (Plautus), Plaure being no name. In Plautus the lines are spoken by the maid Astaphium of men's tongues and hearts; Coras turns them on women.

english.html: And do not excuse yourself by my sisters, nor by my Uncle: for there is no father, mother, Uncle, sisters nor brothers who ought better to know their son, nephew or brother than the wife ought to know the husband. And of the disaster which has befallen our house, no one is to blame but you. Whereupon the commissioners tried to excuse the said de Rols: but at this first meeting could never soften his heart, nor turn him from his austerity. Thus the imposture of the said du Tilh being entirely discovered, and the newcomer received and recognised by all as the sole Martin Guerre: and the trial by this means fully instructed

lines: Nil moueor lachrymis, iſta ſum capus ab arte.
Semper ab inſidiis, Cynthia flere ſoles.
Et à la verité, par ce que les femmes ſemblent eſtre
nées pour plourer, & l'armoyent quand il leur plaiſt &
bon leur ſemble {b},
Diſcunt lachrymare decenter,
Quóq; volunt plorant tempore, quóq; modo {c}.
Il ne faut point donner du tout foy à leurs larmes le
plus ſouuent feintes, ſimulees, & pleines d'hypocriſie,
ni a leus paroles auſſi: car les femmes ont (dit Plau-
te) en leurs langues miel: mais leur cœur eſt tout cou
uert de fiel, arrouſé de vinaigre, plein de toute amer-
tume {d}.
Et ne vous excuſez en mes ſeurs, ni en
mõ Oncle: car il n'y a pere, mere, Oncle,
ſeurs ni freres, qui doyuent mieux co-
gnoiſtre leur fils, nepueu, ou frere que la
femme doit cognoiſtre le mari. Et du
deſaſtre qui eſt auenu à noſtre maiſon,
nul a le tort que vous. Sur quoy les com
miſſaires ſ'eſſayerent excuſer ladite de
Rols: mais en cette premiere rencon-
tre, ne peurent oncques amolir ſon
cueur, ni le diuertir de ſon auſterité.
Ainſi l'impoſture dudit du Tilh, eſtant
entierement deſcouuerte, & le nou-
neau venu de tous vniquement receu,
& recognu pour Martin Guerre: & le
procez par ce moyen du tout inſtruir,
Euripides
in Medea.
Ouid. au iij
de arte amãd.
Plaute en
ſon Tuſcul.
